figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Overview of Open-HumanScale. Using a curated 50,000-hour egocentric corpus, we show that scaling human data improves robot generalization after post-training, with greater task and scene diversity yielding steeper scaling curves. We then extend this pretraining approach to combine human and robot data, finding that hybrid scaling improves zero-shot success in simulation and across 20 real-world tasks.
figures.headline: Human data scaling improves robot generalization, diversity steepens the curves, and hybrid scaling raises zero-shot success on 20 real-world tasks.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Construction of Open-HumanScale-50K. (a) Five data sources and their retained durations. (b) Data curation based on hand visibility, motion stability, and manipulation activity. (c) Cross-source alignment of camera frames, wrist axes, and gripper openness.
figures.headline: Open-HumanScale-50K draws on five sources, filtered by hand visibility, motion stability, and activity, then aligned across camera frames, wrist axes, and gripper openness.
citing_sentences: To support systematic scaling studies and large-scale egocentric pretraining, we build Open-HumanScale-50K, an open corpus from multiple publicly available egocentric datasets (Figure 2).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Model architecture of HumanWAM-Vanilla and experimental protocol. (a) Egocentric pretraining, robot post-training on clean demonstrations, and closed-loop evaluation under clean, scene-ood, and random conditions. (b) Conditioned on language and proprioception, the video and action experts interact through joint masked self-attention. The masks specify visibility among current-frame (C), future-video (F), and action (A) tokens under isolated attention (IA) and inverse-dynamics (IDM) attention.
figures.headline: The model jointly predicts video and actions, with attention masks controlling which tokens can see future frames.
citing_sentences: To study scaling in pure egocentric pretraining, we adopt a unified world–action model backbone and a standardized training and evaluation pipeline (Figure 3).

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: RoboTwin evaluation setup for our egocentric pretraining exploration. We post-train policies exclusively on clean demonstrations and evaluate them under clean, scene-ood, and random conditions.
figures.headline: Policies trained only on clean RoboTwin demonstrations are evaluated under clean, scene-variation, and full-randomization conditions.
citing_sentences: Representative tasks and evaluation conditions are illustrated in Figure 4.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Scaling egocentric pretraining with isolated attention improves in-distribution performance and generalization. Blue dashed lines show least-squares fits of $\mathrm{SR}=a+b\log_{10}H$, where $H$ denotes pretraining hours, with $R^{2}$ reported in each panel. Gray dashed lines denote the baseline without egocentric pretraining. Success rates increase across all three settings, with larger gains on scene-ood and random, indicating that scaling primarily strengthens generalization beyond the demonstration scenes.
figures.headline: Success rises with pretraining hours under isolated attention, with larger gains on out-of-distribution scenes than on clean demonstrations.
citing_sentences: Figure 5 shows that scaling egocentric pretraining with isolated attention consistently improves downstream policy performance on RoboTwin.
The egocentric series uses the scaled-diversity corpora in Figure 5, while the real-robot series draws on AgiBot Beta [1], ABC-130k [2], and our in-house Cobot Magic data as shown in Table 4.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Scaling egocentric pretraining with IDM attention strengthens downstream generalization. Clean success remains high across scales, while scene-ood and random success improve consistently. Blue dashed lines show log-linear scaling fits for the two out-of-distribution settings, with $R^{2}$ reported in the corresponding panels. Gray dashed lines denote the baseline without egocentric pretraining.
figures.headline: With inverse-dynamics attention, clean success stays high across scales while scene and random success improve steadily with pretraining hours.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 6, clean success remains between 87.4% and 89.0% as egocentric pretraining scales from 100 to 50,000 hours.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Scaling egocentric pretraining with growing or fixed task and scene diversity. Blue circles denote scaled-diversity corpora, and orange squares denote matched-diversity corpora. Dashed and dash-dotted lines show the respective least-squares fits of $\mathrm{SR}=a+b\log_{10}H$, with both equations shown in each panel. Scaled-diversity yields a steeper fitted slope in all three settings.
figures.headline: Expanding task and scene diversity with duration yields steeper fitted slopes than adding duration alone at fixed coverage, in all three settings.
citing_sentences: Figure 7 shows that expanding diversity alongside duration produces steeper scaling slopes than increasing duration at fixed coverage.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Scaling egocentric pretraining improves the sample efficiency of robot adaptation. Success rates as a function of the number of robot demonstrations per task for different egocentric pretraining scales.
figures.headline: Robot success rises with larger egocentric pretraining across demonstration counts per task, showing more efficient post-training.
citing_sentences: Figure 8 shows a consistent scaling trend in post-training sample efficiency.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Cross-source action alignment improves downstream policy performance. Aligned and Raw models are pretrained on the same four-source 1,000-hour corpus using aligned and native action representations. Each point reports the best success rate across post-trained checkpoints for the corresponding pretraining run and evaluation setting. Gray dashed lines denote the baseline without egocentric pretraining.
figures.headline: Aligned action representations outperform raw native actions in every setting for the same four-source 1,000-hour pretraining corpus.
citing_sentences: Figure 9 shows that Aligned outperforms Raw at every evaluated pretraining step across all three settings.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Cross-source action alignment reduces pretraining action loss with little change in video loss. Curves show training losses for Aligned and Raw models on the same four-source 1,000-hour corpus.
figures.headline: Aligned action pretraining lowers training action loss while video loss changes little, compared with raw actions on the same corpus.
citing_sentences: The effect of action alignment is also evident during pretraining (Figure 10).

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Human action supervision during egocentric pretraining improves downstream generalization. Models are pretrained on the same 1,000-hour video corpus with 0%, 50%, or 100% human action supervision.
figures.headline: Adding human action supervision to video prediction consistently improves downstream robot policy performance across all three settings.
citing_sentences: Figure 11 shows that learning human motion alongside video prediction consistently improves downstream robot policy performance across all three settings.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: Egocentric pretraining outperforms robot pretraining from 500 to 5,000 hours. Downstream RoboTwin success rates after pretraining on 100, 500, 1,000, and 5,000 hours of egocentric human or robot data. The egocentric series follows the scaled-diversity configuration in Figure 5. Each point reports the best post-training success rate among the evaluated pretraining checkpoints for that scale and setting.
figures.headline: Egocentric pretraining outperforms robot pretraining in all three settings from 500 to 5,000 hours of data.
citing_sentences: Figure 12 shows that egocentric pretraining outperforms robot pretraining in all three settings from 500 to 5,000 hours.

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: From egocentric pretraining to multi-view robot policies. Three view configurations and training routes with or without EgoPro mid-training.
figures.headline: Three view configurations are compared, with and without EgoPro mid-training, for moving from single-view pretraining to multi-view robot policies.
citing_sentences: We compare three configurations for visual conditioning and video prediction, illustrated in Figure 13.

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: Real-robot tasks and visual evaluation conditions.
figures.headline: Four real-robot tasks, paper cup stacking, towel folding, drawer storage, and desk tidying, are shown with their visual evaluation conditions.
citing_sentences: To assess whether the generalization benefits observed in simulation extend to physical robots, we evaluate HumanWAM-Vanilla on paper cup stacking, towel folding, drawer storage, and desk tidying with a Cobot Magic bimanual robot, as shown in Figure 14.

figures.label: Figure 15
figures.caption: Robot pretraining data overview. The top row reports the overall robot pretraining budget. Word clouds summarize selected (a) action and (b) object terms, while the adjacent bars show label-level percentages for the eight most frequent terms in each group. Percentages use all 751 normalized task-collection labels as the denominator.
figures.headline: Robot pretraining data spans approximately 14.6k hours, with action and object terms summarized by frequency across 751 normalized task labels.
citing_sentences: Figure 15 summarizes the overall training scale and the action and object vocabulary of the real-robot recordings.

figures.label: Figure 16
figures.caption: HumanWAM-Goal architecture. (a) Conditioning. An explicit goal image augments language instructions, current and optional historical observations, and the 49-D robot state. (b) Joint rectified-flow sampling. With conditioning tokens held fixed, the shared video-action Generator iteratively predicts video and action velocities via UniPC updates.
figures.headline: HumanWAM-Goal conditions on a goal image and jointly samples future video and actions with a shared generator.
citing_sentences: We therefore introduce HumanWAM-Goal (Figure 16), which augments world-action modeling with explicit visual-goal conditioning [18].

In HumanWAM-Goal, because the clean goal tokens $\mathbf{g}$ directly anchor the target spatial configuration, we replace two-stage cascading with single-stage joint rectified-flow sampling within the shared-parameter Generator (Figure 16).

figures.label: Figure 17
figures.caption: Zero-shot performance under hybrid data scaling. Task success rates and task coverage ($\geq 2\%$ mean success) across six HumanWAM-Goal pretraining configurations on RoboTwin 2.0 (50 Clean and 50 Random episodes per task).
figures.headline: Adding egocentric human data to robot pretraining raises zero-shot Random success and expands task coverage across six configurations.
citing_sentences: Figure 17 tracks zero-shot success rates and task coverage across six independently trained configurations.

figures.label: Figure 18
figures.caption: Task-level zero-shot scaling with human-robot hybrid training. Mean zero-shot success rates (averaged over Clean and Random) across six representative RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with robot data fixed at 14,618 hours and increasing egocentric human data.
figures.headline: Per-task zero-shot success on six representative RoboTwin tasks shows how adding human data affects grasping, contact, and placement skills.
citing_sentences: Figure 18 illustrates how adding human data affects individual manipulation skills across six representative tasks spanning grasping, contact, and spatial placement.

figures.label: Figure 19
figures.caption: Post-trained performance across pretraining scales on RoboTwin 2.0.
figures.headline: After post-training on 50 clean demonstrations per task, RoboTwin 2.0 success is reported for each pretraining scale.
citing_sentences: Figure 19 reports downstream success rates after adapting each pretrained checkpoint on 50 Clean demonstrations per task.
Because this configuration incorporates post-training augmentations beyond the controlled scaling recipe, we report it separately from the scaling curves in Figure 19.

figures.label: Figure 20
figures.caption: Zero-shot real-robot performance stratified by task difficulty. Success rates across easy and hard tasks as egocentric human data are added to a fixed $14,618\,\text{h}$ robot corpus. The vertical dashed line at $60,556\,\text{h}$ highlights the additional gain on hard tasks from robot-balanced batch sampling ($+8\,\text{pp}$).
figures.headline: Zero-shot real-robot success rises with human data on both easy and hard tasks, and robot-balanced batch sampling adds a further gain on hard tasks.
citing_sentences: Figure 20 illustrates how scaling hybrid data affects real-world zero-shot execution across different task difficulties.

figures.label: Figure 21
figures.caption: Per-task zero-shot evaluation on physical robots. Task-level success rates (left) and mean progress scores (right) across all 20 benchmark tasks for the robot-only baseline and three human–robot hybrid configurations.
figures.headline: Per-task zero-shot success and progress across all 20 tasks show hybrid configurations solving tasks the robot-only baseline never completes.
citing_sentences: Figure 21 breaks down zero-shot performance across all 20 benchmark tasks.

figures.label: Figure 22
figures.caption: Qualitative real-robot zero-shot rollouts. Each row pairs the inference-time goal image (left) with four head-camera keyframes from the resulting zero-shot execution (right), showing the initial scene, two intermediate interaction stages, and the final state. The examples span object transport and placement, coordinated bimanual manipulation, object reordering, and multi-step tool/container interactions.
figures.headline: Zero-shot rollouts on eight real-world tasks reach the arrangement in each goal image and include intermediate behaviors the goal does not specify.
citing_sentences: Figure 22 visualizes representative zero-shot rollouts across eight real-world tasks.

figures.label: Figure 23
figures.caption: Visual goal conditioning in pretrained HumanWAM-Goal. Each panel pairs the inference-time goal image (left) with synchronized first-person and third-person keyframes (right). Without target-task post-training or parameter updates, changing the visual goal directs the policy to place the bottle (a) on the tabletop in front of the green block or (b) atop the large purple block.
figures.headline: Changing only the visual goal makes the same pretrained policy place a bottle before a green block or atop a purple block.
citing_sentences: Figure 23 compares two rollouts initialized from the same tabletop scene containing colored blocks, conditioned on visual goals that specify distinct destinations for a bottle.

figures.label: Figure 24
figures.caption: Goal-based in-context learning after post-training for tabletop sorting and stacking. Each panel pairs a supplied goal image (left, blue border) with eight chronological third-person frames (right, read left-to-right across the top then bottom row; green border marks the final state). The goals specify (a) sorting toy cars into the blue bin, plush toys into the white bin, and stacking books near the table center with the green book on top; (b) swapping the toy-to-bin assignments; and (c) retaining the original toy assignments while placing the purple book on top of a stack shifted toward the white bin.
figures.headline: After post-training, the same policy re-sorts toys and re-stacks books when the goal image changes the assignments.
citing_sentences: Figure 24 evaluates a post-trained policy on a multi-object tabletop organization task under three distinct visual goals.

figures.label: Figure 25
figures.caption: Goal-based in-context learning after post-training for office desk organization. Each panel pairs a goal image and enlarged detail view (left) with six ordered third-person execution frames (right). Panels (a, b) redirect the storage of a tape roll and tape measure from the upper drawer to the middle drawer. Panels (c, d) swap the destinations of a glue stick and two pens between the left and right holders (defined in the goal-image frame). Endpoints show item placement prior to drawer closure in (a, b) and after the final pen release in (c, d).
figures.headline: The post-trained office desk policy redirects storage to a different drawer and inverts placement order when the goal image changes.
citing_sentences: Figure 25 further tests paired goal variations in an office workspace involving articulated storage and multi-item sorting.

figures.label: Figure 26
figures.caption: Cross-embodiment in-context learning from egocentric human goal images. Each panel pairs a human-demonstrated goal image and enlarged detail view (left, showing human hands) with synchronized first-person and third-person robot execution frames (right). Panels (a, b) direct the robot to file the brown notebook into the rightmost or leftmost rack slot, respectively. Panels (c, d) specify placing the covered mug near the monitor or beside the file rack. Green borders highlight the completed placements upon gripper release.
figures.headline: Human goal images steer the robot to file notebooks left or right and place a mug near the monitor or beside the rack.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 26, despite the visual domain gap and the presence of human hands in the conditioning images, the policy accurately interprets the underlying spatial relations and adapts its execution across both paired comparisons: it slots the brown notebook into either the rightmost or leftmost compartment before arranging the white notebooks (panels a vs. b), and it caps the mug before transporting it to either the monitor or the file rack (panels c vs. d).

figures.label: Figure 27
figures.caption: Long-horizon desk organization with HumanWAM-Goal. Fourteen chronologically ordered stages from a single continuous rollout, shown through paired first-person (left) and third-person (right) views. The trajectory sequentially executes mug capping and placement, pen and glue-stick sorting, articulated drawer storage of a tape roll and tape measure, and notebook filing. Green borders mark the terminal state after the final notebook is released into the rack.
figures.headline: A single 14-stage rollout on a cluttered desk chains mug capping, sorting, drawer storage, and notebook filing without disturbing earlier placements.
citing_sentences: Figure 27 illustrates a continuous 14-stage rollout on a cluttered office desk.

figures.label: Figure 28
figures.caption: Long-horizon mobile household tidying with HumanWAM-Goal. Twenty-eight chronologically ordered keyframes from a single continuous rollout spanning multiple work areas: sorting tabletop toys and books, navigating to a side table to collect and discard empty bottles, gathering garments from two chairs into a laundry hamper, and returning to the main table.
figures.headline: One continuous rollout across multiple work areas sorts toys, discards bottles, and gathers garments into a hamper.
citing_sentences: Figure 28 extends evaluation from a stationary tabletop to room-scale mobile manipulation on Astribot S1.

abstract: Egocentric human video offers a scalable source of manipulation priors for robot learning, yet translating raw data scale into generalizable robot policies demands rigorous data curation and training recipes. We introduce Open-HumanScale, the first fully open recipe for scaling egocentric pretraining to 50,000 hours, anchored by Open-HumanScale-50K—a curated egocentric video corpus densely annotated with hand motion and natural language. Leveraging this corpus, we systematically investigate pure human pretraining via closed-loop simulation evaluations and uncover an empirical log-linear scaling law linking pretraining data hours to downstream robot success rates. Grounded in these findings, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, a world–action model pretrained exclusively on 50k hours of egocentric human video. Upon robot post-training, HumanWAM-Vanilla reaches 92.08% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, alongside a 14.17% mean success rate and a 19.00 mean progress score on RoboDojo. To push the capability frontier further, we explore joint human–robot pretraining with HumanWAM-Goal, a visual-goal-conditioned world–action model. Hybrid data scaling unlocks broad zero-shot generalization across both simulation and physical benchmarks, propelling post-trained RoboTwin 2.0 performance to new state-of-the-art levels: 92.70% on Clean2Clean and a substantial leap to 84.60% on Clean2Random. On physical robots, HumanWAM-Goal further exhibits emergent embodied in-context learning, dynamically adapting its manipulation behavior to unseen visual goals without parameter updates. To support reproducible scaling research in embodied AI, we open-source the Open-HumanScale-50K corpus, data curation and pretraining pipelines, alongside the pretrained and post-trained HumanWAM checkpoints, inference code, and simulation evaluation suites.

sections.body: The introduction states that egocentric human video can supply manipulation priors, but that pretraining recipes for scaling it remain under investigation. It presents Open-HumanScale, which pretrains on 100 to 50,000 hours of human egocentric data within a unified world–action model framework and evaluates with closed-loop simulation. It reports an empirical log-linear scaling law for out-of-distribution success and presents HumanWAM-Vanilla, which reaches 92.08% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random. HumanWAM-Goal adds joint human–robot pretraining and visual-goal conditioning, reaching 92.70% and 84.60% after post-training. The contributions are a scaling study, the two models, and a release of the corpus, pipelines, and checkpoints.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Egocentric human video is proposed as a scalable source of robot priors, with an open 50,000-hour recipe and two world–action models.

sections.body: The section builds Open-HumanScale-50K from HumanNet, EgoSuite-Open100K, EgoDex, Gen-HumanEgo, and EgoVerse, with the total reported as 50,000.00 hours after curation. The corpus contains 31,396,799 episodes that yield 35,934,235 continuous clips. Curation keeps sequences with usable hand views, splits sequences at unstable action or camera frames, and trims inactivity using 32-frame windows, discarding chunks with fewer than 70% active windows. Actions are mapped into a bimanual end-effector space with positions in meters and unit quaternions, and wrist axes and gripper openness are aligned across sources. For HumanNet, wrist axes are aligned using projected wrist axes and monocular hand landmarks.
sections.heading: Building an Open Egocentric Pretraining Corpus
sections.headline: Open-HumanScale-50K draws on five sources, filters clips for hand visibility, motion stability, and activity, and aligns actions into one bimanual space.

sections.body: The section runs controlled scaling studies on RoboTwin 2.0 with egocentric pretraining from 100 to 50,000 hours. With isolated attention, clean success rises from 71.2% at 100 hours to 80.0% at 10,000 hours, against 69.5% without egocentric pretraining. Scene-ood success rises from 25.2% to 58.1% and random success from 8.4% to 28.7%, against 16.2% and 2.1% without pretraining. The fit $\mathrm{SR}=a+b\log_{10}H$ has $R^{2}$ values of 0.971, 0.949, and 0.877 for clean, scene-ood, and random. Each tenfold increase in hours gives fitted gains of 4.43 pp, 15.88 pp, and 10.24 pp. With inverse-dynamics attention, clean success stays between 87.4% and 89.0%, so clean gains are limited while the out-of-distribution settings still rise.
sections.heading: Exploration of Pure Egocentric Data Scaling
sections.headline: Downstream success follows a log-linear law in pretraining hours, with larger gains under out-of-distribution shifts than in-distribution.

sections.body: The section describes HumanWAM-Vanilla as an inverse-dynamics attention model pretrained for 100,000 optimizer steps on Open-HumanScale-50K with a global batch size of 8,192. Robot post-training for RoboTwin 2.0 uses 2,500 demonstrations and 24,000 optimizer steps. On RoboTwin 2.0, the policy reaches 92.08% on Clean2Clean, the highest value in the compared table, and 68.88% on Clean2Random, for an average of 80.48%. The section states that the remaining gap to the leading world–action models lies in out-of-distribution performance, and that the basic architecture, which has no specialized modules, may partly explain it. Real-robot experiments show gains over a baseline without egocentric pretraining, largest under visual distribution shifts.
sections.heading: Pure Egocentric Data Foundation Model Training
sections.headline: After post-training, HumanWAM-Vanilla reaches 92.08% on Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, below the leading entry's 81.48% on Clean2Random.

sections.body: The section assembles approximately 14.6k hours of robot data, with more than 1.1 million real-robot episodes across eight domains. It extends the action space to 49 dimensions covering joints, chassis, and the 16-dimensional bimanual end-effector action, and it expresses gripper aperture in meters normalized by 0.12 m. HumanWAM-Goal conditions on a language instruction, the current observation, and a goal image, and it predicts 12 future video frames and a 48-step action chunk. It is built on the pretrained Cosmos3-Nano-16B backbone. In simulation, adding 45,938 hours of human data lifts Random success to 74.36%, while Clean stays near 89%, which the section attributes to saturation by target-task demonstrations.
sections.heading: Pushing the Model Capability Boundary with Hybrid Data Scaling
sections.headline: Adding 45,938 hours of human video to a 14,618-hour robot corpus raises Random success from 70.80% to 74.36%, breaking the robot-only plateau.

sections.body: The section evaluates real-robot policies on Astribot S1 with a 20-task zero-shot suite of 10 easy and 10 hard tasks, with 10 trials per task. Each task has weighted progress stages that sum to 10, and binary success is reported alongside. The robot-only baseline reaches 20.0% mean success, rising to 26.0% and 30.5% with added human data, and tasks with at least one success rise from 10/20 to 16/20. Hard-task success reaches 19.0% under standard sampling, and a robot-balanced 1:1 batch ratio raises it to 27.0%. Goal-image experiments show the frozen policy changing its placements with the goal, and 14-stage and 28-keyframe rollouts show long-horizon chaining.
sections.heading: Emerging Capabilities in Real-World Robot Behavior
sections.headline: Hybrid scaling raises real-robot zero-shot success from 20.0% to 30.5% across 20 tasks, and visual goals steer the frozen policy to different outcomes.

sections.body: The section situates the work in three areas. World–action models couple video dynamics prediction with action generation, and they differ in how future visual information enters action prediction; DreamZero learns control through joint video–action modeling. Pure egocentric pretraining work includes EgoScale, which scales action-labeled egocentric pretraining to over 20,000 hours, and HumanScale, which reports a scaling law against validation action loss. Dyna-2 extends human-video pretraining to one million hours. The third area covers in-context learning from demonstrations and visual subgoals, including the π0.7 policy. The section states that this work complements these architectures by studying egocentric data scaling across different world–action configurations.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work groups world–action models, pure egocentric pretraining, and in-context learning, and positions this study as scaling egocentric data across them.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the main claims. Pure egocentric pretraining from 100 to 50,000 hours shows an empirical log-linear scaling law in downstream out-of-distribution success, and task and scene diversity strengthen this trend. Larger pretraining improves the sample efficiency of robot adaptation, and controlled experiments support the value of human motion prediction and cross-source action alignment. HumanWAM-Goal improves zero-shot transfer in simulation and on physical robots, and visual goals enable embodied in-context learning with frozen parameters. The section summarizes these earlier results and the release of data, training code, checkpoints, and evaluation protocols.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Open-HumanScale reports a log-linear out-of-distribution scaling law from human video, and HumanWAM-Goal improves zero-shot and post-trained RoboTwin 2.0 transfer.

sections.body: The appendix describes how goal images for the RoboTwin evaluation are synthesized. A reasoning model grounds task objects in the initial head-camera image, and an image editing model produces a completed-task image. Each generated image is then reviewed and repaired when needed. Of 7,032 newly generated goal images, 6,380 (90.7%) passed the first review, 542 (7.7%) failed, and 110 (1.6%) were uncertain; after repair, all 7,032 passed. The review checks visual and instructional consistency only and does not verify physical feasibility or task success in simulation. The second part lists the ten easy and ten hard real-world tasks, with milestone scores that sum to 10 and a separate binary success outcome.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers goal image synthesis and review for RoboTwin, and the real-world zero-shot task suite with scoring rubrics.
